RagShortTexts: Bosporan leaders bargain over harbours, supplies and armed protection.
Evidence for a uniform fourth-century Bosporan feudal court is lacking.

Variants.Content: Bosporan power rests on the towns and routes around the strait joining the Black Sea to the Maeotis. Harbour access, grain, fish and dealings with neighbouring peoples give local leaders different interests. A ruler needs armed support without driving away the traders and cultivators who sustain that support. Fourth-century evidence is fragmentary, so the module's court should not be presented as a fully documented medieval feudal hierarchy. Its internal disputes can concern access to a landing place, the cost of a guard and which household bears a loss after a raid, rather than identical senatorial conspiracies borrowed from Rome.

A guard at a Bosporan landing watches the water and the approaches from inland. Merchants want cargo moved before bad weather, while his party needs food and a clear promise of pay. An argument between patrons becomes dangerous when it leaves a gate undermanned or a boat waiting offshore with provisions aboard.

A local notable wants the harbour open, but also wants a voice in who collects its dues and supplies its watch. A rival's agreement with an inland chief can change that balance. Prestige depends on sustaining useful connections, not on claiming that every disputed shore is a hereditary fief under one uniform law.
